\section{Model Predictive Path Integral PID Control for Learning-Based Path Following}\label{sec:toru}

\corresponding author. Postal address: Toyota Central R&D Labs., Inc., Nagakute 480-1192, Japan. Phone: +81-90-6384-4818

\noindent\textit{Email address: teruki.kano.tg@mosk.tytlabs.co.jp} (Teruki Kato)

\newpage

\subsection{Abstract}

Classical proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control remains widely used in industrial control systems, while model predictive control (MPC) is actively studied to achieve higher performance for systems with nonlinear dynamics. Model predictive path integral (MPPI) control is a sampling-based MPC method that optimizes control inputs without gradient calculations and can handle non-differentiable models and objective functions. However, conventional MPPI directly samples control-input sequences, which can produce large temporal input increments and causes the optimization dimension to grow with the prediction horizon. This study proposes MPPI-PID control, which uses MPPI to optimize PID gains online instead of directly optimizing the control-input sequences. By replacing high-dimensional input-sequence optimization with low-dimensional gain-space optimization while retaining the PID structure, the proposed formulation improves sampling efficiency and promotes smoother control inputs. Theoretical analyses are provided for a unified path-integral update, the relation between optimization dimension and effective sample size, and the temporal correlation of input perturbations induced by the PID structure. The method is evaluated on a learning-based path following of a mini forklift using a residual-learning dynamics model that combines a physical model and a neural network identified from real-machine driving data. Numerical results show that MPPI-PID improves tracking performance over fixed-gain PID, yields smaller input increments than conventional MPPI, and maintains favorable performance under reduced sampling budgets.

.adjusts the residual contribution depending on the state. This structure follows the concept of learning corrections to a known model, as in universal differential equations [12], while also allowing the residual to be restricted to selected state components [13, 14, 15] or suppressed outside reliable data regions [16].

The physical model is first described in continuous time as follows:

$$ x(t) = f^{\text{phys, c}}(x(t), u(t)). \quad (2) $$

Applying Euler discretization with step size $h$ gives the following:

$$ x_{t+1} = x_t + f^{\text{phys, c}}(x_t, u_t)h =: f^{\text{phys}}(x_t, u_t). \quad (3) $$

For comparison with the residual-learning model, a purely neural discretetime model can also be written as the following:

$$ x_{t+1} = f^{\text{NN}}(x_t, u_t). \quad (4) $$

When some state components are already represented accurately by $f^{\text{phys}}$, the mask $M^{\text{res}}$ allows the neural network to correct only the remaining components. The weighting function $w^{\text{res}}$ enables the model to prioritize the physical formulation in data-scarce regions while using the learned residual in data-rich regions.

2.2. Control

2.2.1. PID control

A PID control computes the control input based on proportional, integral, and derivative operations applied to the deviation of the plant state from a reference state. In this study, we used a multivariable PID controller in which each control-input component could depend on multiple error signals. The control law is the following:

$$ u_{t,j} = u^{\text{bias}}_j + \sum_{l=1}^{n_i^e} \left( K_j^p e_{t,j,l} + K_j^I e_{t,j,l} \sum_{\tau=0}^{t} e_{\tau,j,l}h + K_j^D \frac{e_{t,j,l} - e_{t-1,j,l}}{h} \right). \quad (5) $$

Here, $u_{t,j}$ denotes the $j$-th component of the control input at time $t$, with $u^{\text{bias}}_j$ representing a bias term. $e_{t,j,l}$ denotes the $l$-th error used for the control.

2.2.3. Proposed method: MPPI-based optimization of PID gains
The proposed method optimized the PID-gain vector as follows instead of directly optimizing the control inputs in MPPI:

\[\theta \coloneqq [K_{1,1}^{\text{P}}, K_{1,1}^{\text{I}}, K_{1,1}^{\text{D}}, \ldots , K_{n_{u},n_{u}^{\text{e}}_{u}}^{P}, K_{n_{u},n_{u}^{\text{e}}_{u}}^{I}, K_{n_{u},n_{u}^{\text{e}}_{u}}^{D}]^{T}.\]

Compared with conventional MPPI, the optimization variables were PID gains that remained fixed over the horizon; therefore, the dimension of the decision variables could be significantly reduced. The resulting algorithm is shown in Algorithm 2.

The bold statements indicate the steps that differ from conventional MPPI. As in conventional MPPI, the sample rollouts can be parallelized because each sampled gain vector defines an independent predicted trajectory.

Now we assume that the previous Di list is available as an array of strings, where the current word is accessed via \(l\). Since delegating the computation to the previous list is beneficial owing to the symmetric structure of the network, a bijection \(s: \mathcal{V} \to \mathcal{Y}\) could be defined using \(s[l]\). Dynamic context control for DNNs consists in applying a neural network to the sequence \(s[l]\) to advance the context by a fixed number of words. Consequently, the dependence in the set of context specific to the current word cannot be neglected. Furthermore, Biases ProjectORS often treat the current word as the only unit in a sentence, which is seldom sufficient for word-level tasks. We will show that, even when the length of the current context maximum comes to the last word \(l = \mathcal{V} - 1\), the detailed dependencies in the context may be effective even for sequence-level tasks. This gives us compelling motivation even to study more sophisticated context control mechanisms such as averaged Biases ProjectORS. Intuitively, our model describes the inputs such that, depending on the current position, different Biases ProjectORS shall be triggered to advance the context in different ways. Depending on the context visualization and model configuration, we analyze optimal controls for such models. This involves further research on funneling chains, so the theoretical properties of convergent and diverging state machine approximations of the optimal control problem could possibly partially be captured by the renormalization step, throwing somewhat higher-order derivatives into play. We also show, even without additional information, that each context-specific action should be specified by two contexts variables \(d\) and \(U\), so the support set for each action can, in general, be arbitrarily large. The present work is structured as follows. In Section 2, we cover some background material and review other relevant models. Next, in Section 3, we introduce the context control model and analyze its properties in the most general setting. Subsequently, in Section 4, we analyze how long the exact update cycle remains short in the general case and, for this set of limitations, give near-optimal recursion for the optimal control problem, allowing convergence to \(\pi\) . Section 5 is devoted to the renormalization step in proportional contexts with fixed context size, which may have an effect on the convergence of the series-sum method. Finally, in Section 6, we investigate how long the scope of the context dynamics remains short in several contexts, and analyze in particular how long it remains short the case of very short context sizes. In addition, we show that a quantifier that is perturbed can be inferred from the context.

This subsection describes a simplified analysis that illustrates how the dimension of the optimization variable affects the sample efficiency of the MPPI update rule. As the update in equation (12) corresponds to importance sampling with weights \(w^{(i)}\) , a standard measure of weight degeneracy and sample efficiency is the effective sample size (ESS) [17]. For normalized weights \(\tilde{w}^{(i)} \coloneqq w^{(i)} / \sum_{j = 1}^{I} w^{(j)}\) , the sample ESS is defined as the following:  

\[\tilde{I}^{\mathrm{ESS}} \coloneqq \frac{1}{\sum_{i = 1}^{I} (\tilde{w}^{(i)})^{2}} = \frac{\left(\sum_{i = 1}^{I} w^{(i)}\right)^{2}}{\sum_{i = 1}^{I} (w^{(i)})^{2}}. \quad (19)\]  

Next, we analyzed an idealized counterpart of the preceding quantity, which is given by the following:  

\[I^{\mathrm{ESS}} \coloneqq I \frac{[R_p[w]]^2}{R_p[w^2]}, \quad (20)\]  

The evaluation of \(I^{\mathrm{ESS}}\) requires the first and second moments of the weight \(w\) under \(p\)  

Under the same differentiability and small- perturbation assumptions as in the previous proposition, we approximated the objective function around \(z\) as the following:  

\[J(z + \epsilon) \simeq J(z) + g^T \epsilon , \, g \coloneqq \nabla_z J(z). \quad (21)\]  

Then, the weight in equation (12) becomes the following:  

\[w(\epsilon) = \exp \left(-\frac{J(z + \epsilon)}{\lambda}\right) \simeq \exp \left(-\frac{J(z)}{\lambda}\right) \exp \left(-\frac{g^T\epsilon}{\lambda}\right) =: c \exp \left(-\frac{g^T\epsilon}{\lambda}\right).\]  

As \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma^z)\) , we have the following:  

\[-\frac{g^T\epsilon}{\lambda} \sim \mathcal{N} \left(0, \frac{g^T \Sigma^z g}{\lambda^2}\right), \quad (23)\]  

and hence, \(w(\epsilon)\) follows a log- normal distribution. Therefore, its moments are given by the following:  

\[\mathbb{E}_p[w] = c \exp \left(\frac{1}{2 \lambda^2} g^T \Sigma^z g\right), \, \mathbb{E}_p[w^2] = c^2 \exp \left(\frac{2}{\lambda^2} g^T \Sigma^z g\right). \quad (24)\]

### Page 12

Substituting these into equation (20) yields the following:

\[
I^{\mathrm{ESS}} \simeq I \exp \left( -\frac{1}{\lambda^2} g^T \Sigma^z g \right).
\]
(25)

To make the scaling with the dimension explicit, we assumed the following: the perturbation covariance is isotropic, \(\Sigma^z = (\sigma^z)^2 I_{n_z}\), and each component contributes similarly to the squared gradient norm. Under these assumptions, \(\|g\|^2 \simeq n_z \bar{g}^2\), and hence \(g^T \Sigma^z g \simeq (\sigma^z)^2 n_z \bar{g}^2\). Equation (25) becomes the following:

\[
I^{\mathrm{ESS}} \simeq I \exp \left( -\frac{(\sigma^z)^2 \bar{g}^2}{\lambda^2} n_z \right).
\]
(26)

Equation (26) indicates that the effective sample size can decrease exponentially as the optimization dimension \(n_z\) increases in this idealized setting. Therefore, to maintain \(I^{\mathrm{ESS}}\) at a desired level, the required number of samples \(I\) can grow exponentially with \(n_z\). This argument is not intended to cover cases in which the effective gradient is sparse or otherwise has a special structure that breaks this dimensional scaling. 

In conventional MPPI, the optimization variable is the control-input sequence \(z = [u_0^T, \dots, u_{N-1}^T]^T\) and hence, \(n_z = n_u N\). In contrast to conventional MPPI, in the proposed method, \(z=\theta\) and \(n_z\) equaled the number of PID gains, which was typically small and independent of the horizon length. Consequently, under the same sampling budget \(I\), the proposed method could achieve a larger effective sample size, providing theoretical support for its improved sample efficiency.

From the preceding analysis, the proposed method is expected to yield smaller input increments and smoother control inputs than conventional MPPI.

Remark 1. The aforementioned analysis concerns the control-input sequence generated within the prediction horizon and does not guarantee smooth closed-loop inputs across all control steps. Nevertheless, smoother predicted input sequences are expected to promote smoother applied inputs in a receding-horizon implementation because the first element of each optimized sequence is applied to the plant.

3. Results

This section comprises the mini-forklift application setup, system identification based on real-machine data, and path-following comparisons among the fixed-gain PID control, conventional MPPI, and proposed MPPI-PID method.

3.1. Application to forklift path-following control

3.1.1. State and control input

We consider the motion of a forklift on a two-dimensional plane. Let the state $x_t$ and control input $u_t$ at time $t$ be $x_t = [X_t, Y_t, s_t, c_t, v_t^X, v_t^Y, r_t]^T$, $u_t = [a_t, \delta_t]^T$. Here, $(X, Y)$ denotes the position; $s = \sin(\psi)$ and $c = \cos(\psi)$ are the trigonometric representations of the yaw angle $\psi$; $(v^X, v^Y) = (\dot{X}, \dot{Y})$ is the velocity; and $r = \dot{\psi}$ is the yaw rate. The control input $a$ is the accelerator command, and $\delta$ is the steering angle.

3.4.2. *Evaluation of the sample efficiency, perturbation sensitivity, and computation time*

Next, we evaluated conventional MPPI and MPPI-PID across multiple sample counts, perturbation standard deviations, and random seeds. The settings are summarized in Table 5. The perturbation standard deviations are obtained by multiplying the nominal values listed in Table 4 by 0.5, 1, or 2.

Figure 6 shows the mean path error under each condition. Across all tested sample counts and perturbation standard deviations, MPPI-PID maintains both a small mean path error and low variation across random trials. By contrast, conventional MPPI exhibits larger path errors and higher trial-to-trial variation, particularly when the sample count is small.

Figure 7 shows the mean control-input increment ||Delta;||<sub>2</sub>. For conventional MPPI, a larger perturbation standard deviation tends to produce larger control-input increments, whereas changing the sample count has a smaller effect. MPPI-PID maintains both small control-input increments and low trial-to-trial variation across random trials for all tested conditions. These results agree with the temporal-correlation analysis of the PID-induced input perturbations.
